children.$control__ndgwdnKI8: A 72-hour levain loaf with a deep, blistered crust.

children.text: Our everyday loaf. We feed the levain twice a day, mix it with stone-ground wheat and a little rye, then let the dough rest cold for three days.
The long wait builds a mild tang, an open crumb and a crust that crackles as it cools.

children.$control__ndgwdnKI8: A dense, dark rye with a crackled flour crust.

children.text: Made with rye we mill ourselves each week, soaked overnight with a spoon of malt and baked low and slow.
Slice it thin and keep it for days. It only gets better.

children.text: The pastry that started it all. We laminate the dough by hand with cultured butter over two days.

children.$control__XsajxHioh: Autumn Mornings: What Is New on the Counter

$control__AUdrKiFq2.alt: Autumn Mornings: What Is New on the Counter

children.$control__hJm9lVFWX: What changes in our kitchen when the weather turns, and the bakes we wait all year for.

children.text: You can tell autumn has arrived by the dough. Cooler mornings mean slower proofs, and slower proofs mean more flavour. We lean into it with heavier flours, brown butter and fruit from orchards an hour north of us.
This month the counter fills with pear and hazelnut galettes, spiced morning buns and a dark molasses rye that pairs well with sharp cheese.
Brown your butter until it smells like toffee, cool it completely, and use it anywhere a recipe asks for melted butter. It is the easiest upgrade you can make this season.

children.$control__XsajxHioh: Cold Butter, Warm Hands: Notes on Lamination

$control__AUdrKiFq2.alt: Cold Butter, Warm Hands: Notes on Lamination

children.$control__hJm9lVFWX: Why the temperature of our butter decides whether a croissant flakes or falls flat.

children.text: Two ingredients, one tug of war

Lamination is a negotiation between dough and butter. Both need to bend at the same rate. If the butter is too cold it cracks into shards. Too warm, and it melts into the dough and the layers disappear.
We keep our butter block at around 13°C and the dough a little colder. Each fold is followed by a rest in the fridge, so nothing has time to soften.
What you see in the crumb
Cut a croissant in half. A good one looks like a honeycomb: open, even cells separated by thin, shiny walls. That pattern is a record of every fold.

children.$control__XsajxHioh: A Sunday Sourdough That Fits Into Your Week

$control__AUdrKiFq2.alt: A Sunday Sourdough That Fits Into Your Week

children.$control__hJm9lVFWX: A forgiving schedule for a crusty loaf, built around a normal working week.

children.text: Feed your starter before bed. On Saturday morning, mix 450g bread flour, 50g wholemeal, 375g water and 100g active starter. Rest for an hour, then add 10g salt.
Give the dough four sets of folds over the next two hours, then leave it alone until it has grown by about half. Shape it, place it in a floured basket and refrigerate overnight.
Heat a lidded pot at 250°C for 45 minutes. Bake the cold loaf covered for 20 minutes, then uncovered for 25 more. Wait an hour before slicing. We know. Wait anyway.

children.$control__hJm9lVFWX: The people who light the ovens while the rest of the city sleeps.

children.text: Our day starts at four. By the time the doors open at seven, the team has shaped around six hundred pastries and pulled forty loaves from the deck oven.
Most of our bakers came to us from other careers: a set designer, a nurse, a former line cook. What they share is patience and a slightly worrying love of early alarms.
If you visit before eight, look through the window behind the counter. Someone will probably wave with a floury hand.
